Not every dog can do this, and not every trainer can or should. With the owners' permission, I used Bishop to help communicate a lesson to Ryder. Dogs naturally understand other dogs better than they understand us. The goal wasn't to make Ryder love every dog she sees-it was to teach her that she doesn't need to react to every dog she sees. Before training, a simple neighborhood walk was nearly impossible. Seeing another dog meant lunging, pulling, and trying to start conflict. Through obedience work and carefully controlled sessions with Bishop, Ryder learned a valuable lesson: not every dog is a threat, and not every situation requires a reaction. Also notice how Bishop's corrections increase in intensity throughout the video. He starts with the minimum amount of pressure necessary and only escalates when Ryder chooses not to listen. That's how dogs naturally communicate with one another. Will I tell these owners to take her to a dog park and expect her to be everyone's best friend? Absolutely not. But can we give her a better quality of life by helping her calmly walk past another dog across the street? Absolutely. Not every dog needs this type of training, but some dogs can benefit tremendously from it. Resource guarding can start as early as puppyhood, and if it's ignored, it can become a serious problem as your dog gets bigger and stronger. Puppies that growl, stiffen up, hover over food, toys, beds, or stolen items are showing signs that they may be uncomfortable with people or other dogs approaching their resources. The earlier you identify it, the easier it is to teach your puppy that people coming near their food or toys is a positive thing—not something to fear. Addressing resource guarding early helps prevent bites, fights, and unwanted behavior later in life, especially in powerful breeds. A confident, well-socialized puppy should learn that giving up an item doesn't mean losing it forever—it often means something even better is coming. 🐾💪🏾
